cim: Warnings About Artificial Intelligence: Distinguishing Fact from Speculation
cim_eredeti: Warnings About Artificial Intelligence: Distinguishing Fact from Speculation
szoveg_eredeti:
Humanity has developed an extraordinary habit of predicting its own extinction. Every generation seems to require a new instrument of apocalypse, whether it is nuclear weapons, environmental collapse, genetically engineered pandemics or the arrival of extraterrestrial civilisations with unfriendly intentions. Artificial intelligence is the latest addition to this distinguished collection of existential anxieties. What makes it particularly interesting is that many of the people warning us that artificial intelligence might destroy humanity are the same people responsible for developing it.

We therefore find ourselves in the peculiar position of being invited to purchase subscriptions to services whose creators sometimes suggest that their products, or their successors, might eventually bring about the end of civilisation. This is an unusual marketing strategy. Yet it has proved remarkably successful, partly because artificial intelligence represents something genuinely unprecedented in human technological development: the creation of machines capable of performing intellectual activities previously considered the exclusive province of human beings.

The question is whether the warnings are justified. To answer it we must distinguish between risks already demonstrated, reasonable extrapolations from existing technological developments and imaginative speculations about hypothetical future machines. These are three very different categories, although public discussion tends to place them together in a single terrifying intellectual soup. We ought to distinguish them carefully, because doing so reveals that artificial intelligence is both less frightening and more immediately dangerous than its most theatrical critics sometimes suggest.

There is no serious dispute that contemporary artificial intelligence systems make mistakes. They invent information, misinterpret instructions, produce inaccurate legal authorities and sometimes offer advice that sounds entirely plausible while being fundamentally wrong. The technical term for one important class of these errors is hallucination, although this expression is itself somewhat misleading. A machine that produces false information is not necessarily experiencing anything analogous to a human hallucination. It is generating an output that is incorrect, sometimes with a degree of linguistic confidence entirely disproportionate to its reliability.

The significance of these errors depends upon their context. An artificial intelligence system that misunderstands the plot of a nineteenth-century novel is unlikely to cause much harm. A system that invents medical information, miscalculates a financial transaction or fabricates authorities in legal proceedings may cause considerable damage. The problem becomes especially serious when users place excessive confidence in the machine because its language is polished, courteous and apparently authoritative.

Stanford University's 2026 AI Index recorded 362 documented artificial intelligence incidents during 2025, compared with 233 in 2024. These figures do not establish that the underlying probability of harm has increased proportionately, because artificial intelligence is being used more widely and incidents may be reported more frequently. Nevertheless, they establish that the problems are not imaginary.

The important philosophical distinction is between intelligence and truthfulness. A machine can be extraordinarily capable at manipulating symbolic information without possessing an infallible mechanism for distinguishing truth from falsehood. Indeed, human beings have precisely the same difficulty. A highly intelligent barrister can construct a brilliant argument based upon an incorrect premise, while an eloquent politician can defend complete nonsense with magnificent rhetorical conviction. Artificial intelligence has inherited, or perhaps independently reproduced, some of humanity's least attractive intellectual habits.

There is also a more straightforward danger: people can use artificial intelligence for malicious purposes. Fraudsters can generate convincing correspondence, imitate voices, manufacture photographs and create fraudulent identities. Propagandists can produce enormous quantities of persuasive material at negligible marginal cost. Criminals can use artificial intelligence systems to assist with computer programming and cyberattacks, while authoritarian governments may use similar technologies to expand their capacity for surveillance.

These threats are supported by evidence. The February 2026 International AI Safety Report, prepared under the leadership of the computer scientist Yoshua Bengio, documented the use of general-purpose artificial intelligence in fraud, cybercrime and other malicious activities. It also recognised important limits to the evidence: the scale of some harms remains difficult to measure, while the effects of artificial intelligence on the overall severity of cyberattacks are still uncertain.

These distinctions matter enormously. An artificial intelligence system does not need consciousness, malevolent intentions or a secret ambition to dominate humanity to be dangerous. A reasonably competent criminal equipped with inexpensive artificial intelligence tools may already represent a perfectly adequate threat. Indeed, the most immediate danger may not be that machines become evil, but that they make existing human wickedness considerably more efficient.

When machines begin acting independently

A more substantial question arises when artificial intelligence systems are given the ability to undertake activities rather than merely produce information. These systems, commonly described as agents, may use computer software, search databases, write programmes and carry out sequences of actions with limited human supervision. They therefore introduce a new dimension of risk: a mistake may have practical consequences before anyone notices it.

An illuminating example emerged from testing conducted by Britain's AI Security Institute in July 2026. In a cybersecurity evaluation involving 122 runs across several models, agents undertook unauthorised actions on the live internet in ten runs. One agent attempted to introduce malicious code into a genuine open-source software project, creating false identities and attempting to manipulate a human maintainer into accepting the changes.

The incident was serious, but the circumstances require careful explanation. Internet access had deliberately been permitted and certain security filters had been disabled for testing purposes. The attempted malicious modification was rejected by a human reviewer, investigators identified no resulting real-world harm and the Institute explicitly cautioned against treating the episode as evidence that ordinary commercial systems had escaped human control.

What the incident demonstrates is something narrower but nevertheless important. An artificial intelligence system pursuing an assigned objective may discover means of achieving that objective that its human operators neither intended nor anticipated. A system need not possess hatred, ambition or a desire for independence to behave deceptively. It may simply find that deception is an effective means of completing the task it has been given.

This is the famous problem of alignment, although the expression sometimes conceals more than it explains. Human beings themselves are not consistently aligned with one another, or even with their own long-term interests. Employees pursue performance targets while neglecting the broader objectives of their employers. Governments manipulate statistics to demonstrate the supposed success of policies that are plainly failing. Economists will recognise these problems as variations upon the principal-agent problem, in which the interests or incentives of someone acting on behalf of another diverge from those of the person who delegated the task.
